title: Memory Hierarchy
tagline: Why computers use a pyramid of storage — and how the gap between speed and size shapes every performance decision.

sections.content:
No single memory technology is simultaneously fast, large, and cheap. Registers are lightning fast but hold only a handful of values. Hard drives store terabytes but are thousands of times slower than RAM. The solution is a **hierarchy** — fast-and-small at the top, slow-and-large at the bottom.

Every performance bottleneck you will ever debug traces back to where in this hierarchy your data lives. Understand the hierarchy and cache misses, database tuning, and I/O optimisation all start making sense.

sections.title: Your Desk, Bookshelf, and Library
sections.content: Registers are papers on your desk — instantly in hand. L1/L2 cache is the shelf behind your chair — seconds away. RAM is the filing cabinet across the room — a short walk. SSD is the office library one floor up — a minute's trip. HDD is a warehouse — best retrieved overnight. You keep what you use most on the desk; everything else is retrieved on demand and placed there temporarily.

**Latency vs. capacity tradeoff**: Faster memory requires more complex circuits and more physical space per bit, making it expensive. The hierarchy exploits the fact that programs tend to reuse the same data repeatedly (**temporal locality**) and access nearby memory locations together (**spatial locality**). Caches are designed around these patterns.

**How caches work**: When the CPU requests data, hardware checks L1 first. A **cache hit** returns data in ~1–4 cycles. A **cache miss** escalates to L2, L3, then RAM — each miss adds tens to hundreds of cycles of stall. Data is loaded in fixed-size **cache lines** (typically 64 bytes), so fetching one byte brings the neighbouring 63 bytes too — exploiting spatial locality.

**Practical impact**: Iterating an array sequentially is fast because each cache-line fetch brings the next few elements for free. Jumping around a linked list randomly is slow because each node likely lives in a different cache line — each access is a potential cache miss. This is why flat arrays consistently outperform linked lists in real benchmarks even though big-O complexity is the same.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Both loops do identical work (O(n²) additions) but row-major access is cache-friendly because each Int32Array row is contiguous. Column-major jumps between rows, causing a cache miss nearly every access — visually identical code, dramatically different real-world performance.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: Interview insight: 'Why is a linked list slower than an array for iteration?' — Array elements are contiguous; one cache-line fetch brings multiple elements. Linked-list nodes scatter across memory; each next-pointer dereference is a likely cache miss. Same O(n) complexity, but constant factors differ by 5-10x in practice. This is why cache-friendly data structures are a core systems design concern.

items: Memory hierarchy: Registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM → SSD → HDD — faster = smaller and more expensive per bit.
A cache hit costs ~1 ns; a RAM access costs ~80 ns; an SSD access ~100,000 ns — the gap is enormous.
Cache lines are 64 bytes: one miss loads 64 contiguous bytes, rewarding sequential (spatial locality) access.
Temporal locality (reuse recent data) and spatial locality (access nearby data) are the two principles caches exploit.
Cache-friendly code (array iteration) can be 5-10x faster than cache-unfriendly code (random pointer chasing) at the same algorithmic complexity.

quiz.question: From fastest to slowest, which is the correct order?
options: RAM → L1 Cache → Registers → SSD
Registers → L1 Cache → RAM → SSD
L1 Cache → Registers → RAM → SSD
Registers → RAM → L1 Cache → SSD
quiz.explanation: Registers are fastest (~0.3 ns), then L1 Cache (~1 ns), RAM (~80 ns), and SSD (~0.1 ms). Each level is orders of magnitude slower.

quiz.question: What is a 'cache line'?
options: A pointer to the next cache entry
The fixed-size block of memory loaded on a cache miss (typically 64 bytes)
A single byte stored in L1 cache
The boundary between L1 and L2 cache
quiz.explanation: Cache lines are typically 64 bytes. When any byte in a line is accessed, the entire 64-byte block loads into cache — enabling spatial locality.

quiz.question: What is 'temporal locality'?
options: Accessing memory addresses that are close together
Accessing the same data repeatedly in a short time window
Storing data in time-sorted order
Preloading future instructions
quiz.explanation: Temporal locality means recently used data will likely be used again soon — caches exploit this by keeping recently accessed data in fast storage.

quiz.question: Approximately how much slower is a RAM access compared to an L1 cache hit?
options: 2x
quiz.explanation: L1 hit ~1 ns, RAM ~80 ns — about 80x slower. This gap is why cache misses are a primary performance concern.

quiz.question: Why does iterating a 2D array row-by-row perform better than column-by-column?
options: Row-major has fewer total operations
Row-major access is sequential in memory, hitting the same cache lines repeatedly
Column-major requires more comparisons
Rows are stored in registers automatically
quiz.explanation: Arrays are stored row-by-row (row-major). Row iteration is sequential — cache-friendly. Column iteration jumps large strides, causing a cache miss on almost every access.

quiz.question: What is 'spatial locality'?
options: Accessing the same address repeatedly
Accessing memory addresses near recently accessed addresses
Storing variables close to the CPU
Distributing data across multiple cache levels
quiz.explanation: Spatial locality: if you access address X, you'll likely access X+1, X+2 … soon. Cache lines exploit this by fetching 64 bytes at once.

quiz.question: Which storage level typically has the largest capacity?
options: L3 Cache
RAM
L1 Cache
HDD
quiz.explanation: HDD can store 2–20+ TB — by far the largest capacity in the hierarchy, but also the slowest (~10 ms access).

quiz.question: Why is random access through a linked list slower than array iteration, even at the same O(n) complexity?
options: Linked lists use more total memory
Each node pointer dereference likely causes a cache miss due to scattered memory layout
Linked list traversal requires more CPU instructions
Arrays are stored in registers automatically
quiz.explanation: Linked list nodes scatter in memory; each next-pointer dereference jumps to a likely-uncached location, causing repeated cache misses. Arrays are contiguous, so one cache line covers multiple elements.

quiz.question: How many bytes does a typical cache line hold?
quiz.explanation: Modern CPUs use 64-byte cache lines. Fetching one byte pulls in the neighbouring 63 bytes, benefiting sequential access patterns.

quiz.question: What is the primary reason for the memory hierarchy (multiple levels of cache)?
options: Fast memory is physically large and cheap to manufacture
No single technology can be simultaneously fast, large, and inexpensive
CPUs cannot directly access RAM
Operating systems require separate memory levels for security
quiz.explanation: There is a fundamental tradeoff: fast SRAM (used in caches) is expensive and physically dense; slow DRAM (RAM) is cheap and large. The hierarchy uses both, placing frequently accessed data in fast-but-small levels.
